claim: Approximately 600 cancer cell lines were analyzed in this study.
source: Here, we report the chromosomal evolution in ~ 600 cancer cell lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of cell lines studied.

claim: Many cancer cell lines jettisoned either Y or the inactive X chromosome.
source: Many of them jettisoned either Y or the inactive X; thus, free-living male and female cells converge by becoming 'de-sexualized'.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the study's data.

claim: Free-living male and female cells converge by becoming 'de-sexualized'.
source: Many of them jettisoned either Y or the inactive X; thus, free-living male and female cells converge by becoming 'de-sexualized'.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed loss of sex chromosomes.

claim: The active X often doubled in cancer cell lines, accompanied by the addition of one haploid complement of autosomes.
source: Surprisingly, the active X often doubled, accompanied by the addition of one haploid complement of autosomes, leading to an X:A ratio of 2:3 from the extant ratio of 1:2.
evidence: The abstract reports this observation from the data analysis.

claim: The X:A ratio evolved from 1:2 to 2:3 in many cancer cell lines.
source: Surprisingly, the active X often doubled, accompanied by the addition of one haploid complement of autosomes, leading to an X:A ratio of 2:3 from the extant ratio of 1:2.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Theoretical modeling suggests that the 2:3 X:A ratio confers a higher fitness.
source: Theoretical modeling of the frequency distribution of X:A karyotypes suggests that the 2:3 ratio confers a higher fitness and may reflect aspects of sex chromosome evolution.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion from modeling work.

claim: The 2:3 X:A ratio may reflect aspects of sex chromosome evolution.
source: Theoretical modeling of the frequency distribution of X:A karyotypes suggests that the 2:3 ratio confers a higher fitness and may reflect aspects of sex chromosome evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the abstract.

claim: Genomes of multi-cellular organisms evolve to ensure the survival and reproduction of the whole organisms.
source: Genomes of multi-cellular organisms evolve to ensure the survival and reproduction of the whole organisms.
evidence: This is a statement based on established evolutionary biology principles.

claim: Hundreds of cell lines survive as free-living cells that are not organized into tissues, organs or individuals with human interventions.
source: With human interventions akin to domestication, hundreds of cell lines survive as free-living cells that are not organized into tissues, organs or individuals (Alberts et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact with a citation.

claim: Evolution in a quasi-unicellular state may be very different from evolution as multi-cellular entities.
source: Evolution in such a quasi-unicellular state may be very different from the evolution as multi-cellular entities.
evidence: This is a logical inference about evolutionary dynamics.

claim: Most cell lines are cancerous in origin but a few are derived from normal tissues.
source: Most cell lines are cancerous in origin but a few are derived from normal tissues (Hayflick, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Cell lines have evolved characteristics for survival in the unicellular state that is distinct from their natural environments.
source: Regardless of their origin, they have all evolved characteristics for survival in the unicellular state that is distinct from their natural environments.
evidence: This is an inference about adaptation in cell culture.

claim: Cell lines derived from cancer tissues are usually karyotypically less stable than normal cell lines.
source: Cell lines derived from cancer tissues are usually karyotypically less stable than normal cell lines (Lengauer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Karyotypic instability permits cancer cell lines to evolve new karyotypes, including polyploidy, more readily than normal cell lines could.
source: While this instability may impose a cost, it also permits cancer cell lines to evolve new karyotypes, including polyploidy, more readily than normal cell lines could.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary consequences of instability.

claim: Tumorigenesis has been increasingly viewed as a process of evolution, rather than merely pathological conditions.
source: Tumorigenesis has been increasingly viewed as a process of evolution, rather than merely pathological conditions (Nowell, 1976; Merlo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The 'ultra-microevolutionary process' of tumorigenesis is subjected to similar rules including mutation, genetic drift, migration and selection that govern organismal evolution.
source: This 'ultra-microevolutionary process' is subjected to similar rules including mutation, genetic drift, migration and selection that govern organismal evolution (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Cell lines in the cultured state will continue to evolve after the organism dies.
source: While this process usually ends when the organism dies, cell lines in the cultured state will continue to evolve.
evidence: This is a logical inference about cell culture evolution.

claim: Cultured cell lines may be informative about the evolutionary potentials at the cellular level.
source: Much like the diversity unleashed by domestication, cultured cell lines, which can be considered 'domesticated', may be informative about the evolutionary potentials at the cellular level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the value of studying cell lines.

claim: Gene dosage has been observed to change extensively in cancer cell lines as polyploidy, aneuploidy and various copy number variations are common.
source: In this quasi-unicellular state, gene dosage has been observed to change extensively as polyploidy, aneuploidy (full or partial) and various copy number variations (CNVs) are common in cancer cell lines (Roschke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Somatic cells have an inactive X chromosome in females and a Y chromosome in males.
source: Somatic cells have an inactive X chromosome in females and a Y chromosome in males (Charlesworth, 1991).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in genetics with a citation.

claim: 620 cancer cell lines were analyzed using SNP arrays.
source: In this study, we analyze 620 cancer cell lines that have been genotyped using SNP arrays (Greenman et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the data source with a citation.

claim: Among the 620 cancer cell lines, 279 are derived from female tissues and 341 from male tissues.
source: Among them, 279 are derived from female tissues and 341 from male tissues.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data composition.

claim: The elimination of the Y and the inactive X chromosome was observed in cancer cell lines.
source: We observed the elimination of the Y and the inactive X chromosome, followed by the evolution toward a new equilibrium with two active X chromosomes and 3 sets of autosomes (2X:3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: Cancer cell lines evolved toward a new equilibrium with two active X chromosomes and 3 sets of autosomes (2X:3A).
source: We observed the elimination of the Y and the inactive X chromosome, followed by the evolution toward a new equilibrium with two active X chromosomes and 3 sets of autosomes (2X:3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: The most common form of genomic changes in cell lines is the loss of heterozygosity (LOH) when one of the two homologous chromosomes is eliminated.
source: The most common form of genomic changes in cell lines is the loss of heterozygosity (LOH) when one of the two homologous chromosomes is eliminated (Roschke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The percentages of LOH for autosomes are remarkably similar between sexes, with a correlation coefficient of 0.94 among 620 cell lines.
source: For autosomes, the percentages of LOH are remarkably similar between sexes, with a correlation coefficient of 0.94 among 620 cell lines.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: There is a slight tendency for the smaller autosomes to have higher LOH rate (R =~−0.4, p=~0.046).
source: There is a slight tendency for the smaller autosomes to have higher LOH rate (R =~−0.4, p=~0.046, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data with reference to a figure.

claim: The median percentage of LOH is about 13% for autosomes.
source: The median percentage of LOH is about 13% for autosomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data.

claim: The losses of X (37% in females) and Y (40% in males) stand out compared to autosomes.
source: However, the losses of X (37% in females) and Y (40% in males) stand out.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: It is the inactive X (Xi) that is eliminated in female cell lines.
source: Since the expression from the X is not lost, we infer that it's the inactive X(or Xi) that is eliminated.
evidence: This is an inference based on expression data.

claim: Female lines lose the inactive X (Xi) and male lines lose the Y chromosome at a higher rate than other chromosomes.
source: Female lines lose the inactive X (Xi) and male lines lose the Y chromosome at a higher rate than other chromosomes.
evidence: This summarizes the LOH findings for sex chromosomes.

claim: The two sexes may be expected to converge toward having a single sex chromosome.
source: The two sexes may thus be expected to converge toward having a single sex chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed loss patterns.

claim: Long-term cultures might evolve to complete LOH for sex chromosomes as well as autosomes.
source: Furthermore, given that spontaneous LOH is not infrequent and the loss cannot be regained, long-term cultures might evolve to complete LOH for sex chromosomes as well as autosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about long-term evolution.

claim: The genome-wide low rate of LOH suggests selection holding back such changes.
source: The genome-wide low rate of LOH suggests selection holding back such changes.
evidence: This is an inference about the role of selection.

claim: The strong correlation between sexes in LOH rates reflects a balance between the production and elimination of LOH's, likely involved natural selection.
source: The strong correlation between sexes further reflects a balance between the production and elimination of LOH's, likely involved natural selection.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary dynamics.

claim: An extra X chromosome is often gained accompanying the loss of the Y or Xi.
source: A most unexpected finding is that, accompanying the loss of the Y or Xi, an extra X chromosome is often gained.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: Approximately equal numbers of male cell lines have one or two X chromosomes.
source: Figure 1B shows approximately equal numbers of male cell lines with one or two X chromosomes (partial X aneuploidy not counted).
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The extra X in male cell lines is active because the inactivating XIST lncRNA is silenced.
source: This extra X is active because the inactivating XIST lncRNA is silenced in male cell lines (Figure 1C), consistent with previous findings (Guttenbach et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a finding based on XIST expression data with citation.

claim: XIST does not become activated in free-living cells that do not already express this.
source: XIST does not become activated in free-living cells that do not already express this.
evidence: This is an observation about XIST expression patterns.

claim: The expression of X-linked genes is higher in male lines with two X's than in those with one X.
source: The expression of X-linked genes is higher in those male lines with two X's than in those with one X and the up-regulation occurs along the length of the X chromosome (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The up-regulation of X-linked genes occurs along the length of the X chromosome in male lines with two X's.
source: The expression of X-linked genes is higher in those male lines with two X's than in those with one X and the up-regulation occurs along the length of the X chromosome (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Female lines with LOH of the whole X chromosome rarely express XIST.
source: Figure 1E shows that female lines with LOH indeed rarely express XIST, presumably because LOH lines that survive lost the inactive X and kept the active Xa.
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 1E with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Non-LOH female lines tend to express XIST.
source: In contrast, non-LOH lines tend to express XIST, thus obscuring the counting of Xa's.
evidence: This is an observation about XIST expression in non-LOH lines.

claim: Of the 103 LOH female lines, 30 lines have single Xa and 31 lines have whole extra X's.
source: Of the 103 LOH female lines, 30 lines have single Xa and 31 lines have whole extra X's as shown in Figure 1F.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Roughly half of female LOH lines have gained an extra Xa, similar to male lines.
source: Much like male lines of Figure 1B, Figure 1F also shows roughly half of female lines to have gained an extra Xa.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between male and female lines.

claim: Cancer cell lines usually have high rates of aneuploidy and could be heterogeneous within a given line.
source: Cancer cell lines usually have high rates of aneuploidy and could be heterogeneous within a given line, thus making its status difficult to assess.
evidence: This is a statement about a known characteristic of cancer cell lines.

claim: A549 is a male cell line from adenocarcinomic alveolar basal epithelium.
source: The two lines are A549 (a male cell line from adenocarcinomic alveolar basal epithelium) and HeLa (a female cervical cancer cell line).
evidence: This is a description of the cell line used.

claim: HeLa is a female cervical cancer cell line.
source: The two lines are A549 (a male cell line from adenocarcinomic alveolar basal epithelium) and HeLa (a female cervical cancer cell line).
evidence: This is a description of the cell line used.

claim: Neither A549 nor HeLa line expresses XIST, suggesting that all X chromosomes are active.
source: Neither line expresses XIST (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that all X chromosomes are active.
evidence: This is a finding from expression data with an inference.

claim: Almost all A549 and HeLa cells have two or more active X chromosomes.
source: While there is a modest degree of heterogeneity within each line, almost all cells have two or more active X chromosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis.

claim: Within-cell line heterogeneity does not seem to undermine the study's conclusions.
source: While labor intensity of assays and cell availability limited our sample size, we nevertheless can conclude that within-cell line heterogeneity does not seem to undermine our conclusions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the data quality and its impact.

claim: The 'expression phenotype' is expected to change with an extra copy of the active X.
source: With an extra copy of the active X, the 'expression phenotype' is expected to change.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of X chromosome gain.

claim: EX/A has been reported to be around 0.5 ~ 0.8 for normal mammalian tissues.
source: EX/A has been reported to be around 0.5 ~ 0.8 for normal mammalian tissues (Xiong et al., 2010; Deng et al., 2011; Kharchenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: EX/A distributions center on ~ 0.84 in normal cell lines and on one in cancerous cell lines.
source: Figure 3A shows that EX/A distributions center on ~ 0.84 in normal cell lines and on one in cancerous cell lines.
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EX/A ranges from 0.78 to 1.05 in normal cell lines by varying the threshold for counting expressed transcripts.
source: By varying the threshold (Figure 3B), EX/A ranges from 0.78 to 1.05 in normal cell lines but is consistently higher by approximately 15% in cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis with different thresholds shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EX/A is consistently higher by approximately 15% in cancer cell lines compared to normal cell lines.
source: By varying the threshold (Figure 3B), EX/A ranges from 0.78 to 1.05 in normal cell lines but is consistently higher by approximately 15% in cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a comparative finding shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The same pattern of higher EX/A in cancer cell lines is seen in the RNA-seq data.
source: The same pattern is seen in the RNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This confirms the finding using a different data type.

claim: Autosomes should also evolve while sex chromosomes evolve.
source: While sex chromosomes evolve, autosomes should also evolve.
evidence: This is a logical inference about genome evolution.

claim: A key question is whether selection operates on the autosomes as a set.
source: Since the generation of aneuploidy may happen independently for each autosome, a key question is whether selection operates on the autosomes as a set.
evidence: This frames a research question addressed in the study.

claim: Cancerous cell lines acquire autosomes during evolution.
source: Apparently, cancerous cell lines acquire autosomes during evolution.
evidence: This is an inference from the chromosome number distribution.

claim: The distribution of ploidy (n = 22) number shows peaks at 2 and 3.
source: The distribution of ploidy (n = 22) number shows peaks at 2 and 3, indicates that many cell lines appear to be in transition between full diploidy and triploidy of 44 and 66 autosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from the chromosome number distribution analysis.

claim: Many cell lines appear to be in transition between full diploidy and triploidy of 44 and 66 autosomes.
source: The distribution of ploidy (n = 22) number shows peaks at 2 and 3, indicates that many cell lines appear to be in transition between full diploidy and triploidy of 44 and 66 autosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the chromosome number distribution.

claim: The majority of sublines of HeLa cells have 55–75 chromosomes centering about the triploid count of 69.
source: Similarly, the majority of sublines of HeLa cells we examined have 55–75 chromosomes centering about the triploid count of 69 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from HeLa subline analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Autosomes appear to exist as a full complement with n = 22.
source: Indeed, autosomes appear to exist as a full complement with n = 22.
evidence: This is an inference from the chromosome number patterns.

claim: Cells most likely add one autosome at a time.
source: Although autosomes may evolve as a set, cells most likely add one autosome at a time.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of chromosome gain.

claim: Smaller chromosomes are more erratic in their numbers in cell lines.
source: Smaller chromosomes are indeed more erratic in their numbers in cell lines.
evidence: This is an observation from the chromosome analysis.

claim: Only the largest 14 chromosomes (13 autosomes and X), which together account for ~75% of the genome, are used to test the convergence of autosomes.
source: Only the largest 14 chromosomes (13 autosomes and X), which together account for ~75% of the genome, are used to test the convergence of autosomes.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the analysis.

claim: Chromosome 13 is the largest autosome yielding viable trisomic new-borns.
source: The cutoff is based on the observation that chromosome 13 is the largest autosome yielding viable trisomic new-borns (Taylor, 1968; Patterson, 2009; Kleijer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: If whole organisms can survive trisomy, the fitness consequence of the particular aneuploidy would probably be very small at the cellular level.
source: We reason that, if whole organisms can survive trisomy, the fitness consequence of the particular aneuploidy would probably be very small at the cellular level.
evidence: This is a logical inference about fitness effects.

claim: In all 6 HeLa sublines, each of the 13 autosomes has 2–4 copies, ranging from an average of 2.62 to 3.23.
source: In all 6 lines, each of the 13 autosomes has 2–4 copies, ranging from an average of 2.62 to 3.23 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the HeLa subline analysis.

claim: The data suggest that each autosome increases by one copy and only after all of the 13 autosomes have gained an extra copy do further increases continue.
source: The data suggest that each autosome increases by one copy and only after all of the 13 autosomes have gained an extra copy do further increases continue.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the chromosome gain patterns.

claim: The pattern of chromosome gain is statistically significant (p=0.0021 by the χ2 test) with an excess at x = 1.
source: The pattern, like that of Figure 4B, is statistically significant (p=0.0021 by the χ2 test) with an excess at x = 1.
evidence: This is a statistical finding supporting the coordinated chromosome gain.

claim: The larger autosomes evolve cohesively as a set.
source: These results suggest that the larger autosomes evolve cohesively as a set.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the chromosome gain analysis.

claim: With autosomes evolving as a cohesive unit, X:A can be represented by whole numbers of 1:2, 2:3 etc.
source: With autosomes evolving as a cohesive unit, X:A can be represented by whole numbers of 1:2, 2:3 etc.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of coordinated autosome evolution.

claim: Most cell lines have the C(1:2) or C(2:3) genotype which together account for 2/3 of the lines.
source: Shown in Figure 4D, most lines have the C(1:2) or C(2:3) genotype which together account for 2/3 of the lines.
evidence: This is a finding from the C(Xa:A) distribution shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The common occurrence of C(1:2) at 37.4% is not surprising given that it is the starting genotype.
source: Given that C(1:2) is the starting genotype, its common occurrence at 37.4% is not surprising.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genotype frequency.

claim: The high frequency of C(2:3) is unexpected.
source: The high frequency of C(2:3), however, is unexpected.
evidence: This is a statement about the surprising nature of the finding.

claim: To reach C(2:3) from C(1:2), cells should evolve to either C(2:2) or C(1:3) first, but neither genotype is commonly seen.
source: To reach C(2:3) from the starting point of C(1:2), cells should evolve to either C(2:2) or C(1:3) first, but neither genotype is commonly seen in these cells lines.
evidence: This is an observation about the evolutionary pathway.

claim: C(2:3) at 29.2% is the second most common genotype.
source: In contrast, C(2:3) at 29.2% is the second most common genotype.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the genotype distribution.

claim: If we include C(2:4) and C(3:3), the inclusive C(2:3) cluster is the most common genotype.
source: If we include the two genotypes, C(2:4) and C(3:3), that are derivatives of C(2:3), this inclusive C(2:3) cluster is the most common genotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genotype distribution.

claim: The fitness of each genotype, W, is assumed to be determined by the Xa/A ratio.
source: The fitness of each genotype, W, is assumed to be determined by the Xa/A ratio.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption.

claim: One would expect the wild type (W1) to be the fittest genotype.
source: In general, one would expect the wild type (W1) to be the fittest genotype and we particularly wish to know whether that is indeed the case here.
evidence: This is a standard expectation in evolutionary biology.

claim: Under strict neutrality where all nodes have the same fitness, the relative frequency should be in the descending order of C(1:2), C(2:2) and C(2:3) when T >> 0.
source: By - Equation 2, x1(T) > x2(T) > x3(T) when T >> 0. In short, the relative frequency should be in the descending order of C(1:2), C(2:2) and C(2:3) if there is no fitness difference among genotypes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the neutral model.

claim: The predicted inequality at T >> 0 under neutrality is very different from the observed trend.
source: This predicted inequality at T >> 0 is very different from the observed trend.
evidence: This is a comparison between model prediction and observation.

claim: The observed high frequency of the C(2:3) cluster (x3 = 0.482 vs. x1 = 0.41 and x2 = 0.092) is incompatible with a neutrally evolving model of chromosome numbers.
source: Therefore, the observed high frequency of the C(2:3) cluster (x3 = 0.482 vs. x1 = 0.41 and x2 = 0.092) is incompatible with a neutrally evolving model of chromosome numbers.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the model with observations.

claim: The discrepancy between neutral model and observation is true at all time points and is more pronounced at smaller T's.
source: The discrepancy is true at all time points and is more pronounced at smaller T's.
evidence: This is an observation about the model-data comparison.

claim: s < 0 is necessary for x2 to be smaller than x3 in the 4-genotype model.
source: Equation S3 shows that s < 0 is necessary for x2 to be smaller than x3, and t > 0 is necessary for x3 to be close to x1 (see Supplement).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: t > 0 is necessary for x3 to be close to x1 in the 4-genotype model.
source: Equation S3 shows that s < 0 is necessary for x2 to be smaller than x3, and t > 0 is necessary for x3 to be close to x1 (see Supplement).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling.

claim: The extant state in multicellular organisms of C(1:2) is not the fittest genotype for free-living mammalian cells.
source: In conclusion, it appears that the extant state in multicellular organisms of C(1:2) is not the fittest genotype for free-living mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling and data analysis.

claim: The observed genotypic distributions suggest that C(2:3) may have a higher fitness than the wild type, C(1:2).
source: The observed genotypic distributions suggest that C(2:3) may have a higher fitness than the wild type, C(1:2).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling and data analysis.

claim: Free-living mammalian cells speed up evolution when the environment changes.
source: Free-living mammalian cells like all living things speed up the evolution when the environment changes.
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary dynamics.

claim: The practice of cell culturing is to slow down the evolution to preserve cell lines' usefulness as proxies for the source tissues.
source: The practice of cell culturing, however, is to slow down the evolution to preserve cell lines' usefulness as proxies for the source tissues.
evidence: This is a statement about cell culture practices.

claim: Changes in cell lines are inevitable.
source: Nevertheless, changes are inevitable and the evolution of sex chromosomes is but one example.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell line evolution.

claim: Cell lines derived from normal tissues generally do not undergo karyotypic changes at an appreciable rate.
source: Cell lines derived from normal tissues generally do not undergo karyotypic changes at an appreciable rate (Shirley et al., 2012; Frazer et al., 2007; Pickrell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Normal cell lines are much less responsive to selection in cultured conditions that favor new karyotypes.
source: They are therefore much less responsive to selection in cultured conditions that favor new karyotypes.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary potential of normal cell lines.

claim: Cancer cell lines have generally experienced stronger selection more frequently than normal cell lines.
source: Cancer cell lines, having been through more rounds of passages, have generally experienced stronger selection more frequently than normal cell lines.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary history of cancer cell lines.

claim: The extant X:A relationship (C(1:2)) may not be optimal for free-living mammalian cells.
source: Our observations suggest that the extant X:A relationship (C(1:2)) may not be optimal for free-living mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The highest fitness peak appears to be closer to the karyotype of C(2:3) as free-living cells reproducibly evolve toward this new karyotype.
source: The highest fitness peak, instead, appears to be closer to the karyotype of C(2:3) as free-living cells reproducibly evolve toward this new karyotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The fitness peaks in free-living cells being different from that of the multi-cellular organisms is not unexpected.
source: The fitness peaks in free-living cells being different from that of the multi-cellular organisms is not unexpected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in evolutionary context.

claim: The interest of the cellular community may lie in its ability to regulate the growth potential of its constituents.
source: With many possible conflicts between individual cells and the community of cells (i.e., the organism), the interest of the community may lie in its ability to regulate the growth potential of its constituents.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about multicellular organization.

claim: Free-living cells are driven by selection to realize their individual proliferative capacity relative to other cells.
source: Free-living cells, on the other hand, are driven by selection to realize their individual proliferative capacity relative to other cells.
evidence: This is an inference about selection in free-living cells.

claim: The convergence among many cell lines to C(2:3) is unexpected in the context of cancer evolution.
source: The convergence among these many cell lines to C(2:3) is unexpected in the context of cancer evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the surprising nature of the finding.

claim: The TCGA project has shown that cancer evolution is a process of divergence, not convergence.
source: The TCGA project (reference) has shown that cancer evolution is a process of divergence, not convergence.
evidence: This is stated as a known finding from TCGA.

claim: Only two genes have been mutated in more than 10% of all cancer cases.
source: Indeed, only two genes have been mutated in more than 10% of all cancer cases and tumors of the same tissue origin from two different patients may often share no mutated genes at all (Wu et al., 2016; Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Tumors of the same tissue origin from two different patients may often share no mutated genes at all.
source: Indeed, only two genes have been mutated in more than 10% of all cancer cases and tumors of the same tissue origin from two different patients may often share no mutated genes at all (Wu et al., 2016; Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The karyotypic convergence reported in this study is rather unusual.
source: Therefore, the karyotypic convergence reported here is rather unusual.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the finding.

claim: C(2:3) toward which cultured cells evolved happens to be the smallest possible increase in the X/A ratio from C(1:2).
source: We note that C(2:3) toward which cultured cells evolved happens to be the smallest possible increase in the X/A ratio from C(1:2).
evidence: This is an observation about the evolutionary trajectory.

claim: The higher fitness of C(2:3) than C(1:2) in free-living cells may lend new clues to the debate about the evolution of mammalian sex chromosomes.
source: The higher fitness of C(2:3) than C(1:2) in free-living cells may lend new clues to the debate about the evolution of mammalian sex chromosomes (Kharchenko et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: With X-inactivation, it has been suggested that EX/A could have been reduced, or even halved.
source: With X-inactivation, it has been suggested that EX/A could have been reduced, or even halved (Xiong et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The observation that free-living cells continue to evolve toward C(2:3) raised the possibility that the evolutionary increase in EX/A has not been complete, in comparison with the ancestral EX/A.
source: Our observation that free-living cells continue to evolve toward C(2:3) raised the possibility that the evolutionary increase in EX/A has not been complete, in comparison with the ancestral EX/A.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The common view posits that individual cells in tumors evolve to enhance self-interest.
source: The common view that tumorigenesis is an evolutionary phenomenon posits that individual cells in tumors evolve to enhance self-interest (Nowell, 1976; Merlo et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2015; Chen and He, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A corollary would be that tumorigenesis may have taken the first few steps toward uni-cellularity.
source: A corollary would be that tumorigenesis may have taken the first few steps toward uni-cellularity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the evolutionary view of cancer.

claim: This extended view is supported by many expression studies as well as the higher likelihood of obtaining cell lines from tumors than from normal tissues.
source: This extended view is supported by many expression studies as well as the higher likelihood of obtaining cell lines from tumors than from normal tissues (Hayflick, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: An alternative view posits that tumors remain multi-cellular in organization.
source: An alternative view, posits that tumors remain multi-cellular in organization (Almendro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: It is possible that cancer cells in vivo may have been gradually evolving toward a new optimum.
source: It is possible that cancer cells in vivo may have been gradually evolving toward a new optimum.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about cancer evolution.

claim: Cancer cells in men and women are converging in their sex chromosome evolution and become more efficient in proliferation in this new de-sexualized state.
source: In that case, cancer cells in men and women are converging in their sex chromosome evolution and become more efficient in proliferation in this new de-sexualized state.
